issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Duc, a thirty-one-year-old carpenter, was on his way home from a job site late one evening when he was pulled over by two officers. The stop escalated within seconds. He remembered the hard pressure of a knee on his neck, the concrete against his cheek, the sound of his own voice trying to explain he had done nothing wrong. He was released without charges, but something inside him had been pinned to the ground that night and never got up.

In the weeks that followed, Duc began to notice a constant sense of unease that he could not shake. At his workshop, he found himself instinctively backing into corners, positioning his workbench so that his back was against a wall and he could see the entire room. If a supplier arrived late or a nail gun jammed, his chest would tighten and he would assume the worst—that something terrible was about to happen, that he was about to be blamed or caught. He could not relax, even at home with his wife, even when he knew logically that he was safe. That persistent vigilance drained him, and soon he started to cope in ways he had never needed before. On the drive to work, he would replay the night over and over, mentally listing every thing he could have done differently: maybe if he had kept his hands more visible, if he had not reached for his wallet so quickly, if he had stayed quieter. This self-blame became a loop that felt like punishment but also, perversely, like a way to gain control—if he could figure out his own mistake, maybe he could avoid it next time. Those rumination sessions often left him feeling more trapped and vulnerable, not less. When the thoughts grew unbearable, he began using marijuana after work, just enough to blur the edges. He also started deliberately avoiding any thought about the event itself, switching the channel in his mind the moment it surfaced. But these strategies only tightened the cycle: the more he tried to push the memory away, the more hypervigilant he became; the more he used drugs, the harder it was to relax in a safe setting; the deeper he sank into self-blame, the more convinced he grew that danger was everywhere, that he had to stay on guard because he could not trust himself to handle a situation properly.

Over months, this pattern carved a groove into his daily life. At the job site, his coworkers noticed he was jumpy and withdrawn; he stopped joining them for lunch in the open bay, instead eating alone with his back to a pillar. Minor delays on a project—a missing shipment, a power outage—would send him into a spiral of silent panic, and he would retreat to the bathroom to compose himself. His wife grew concerned. She told him he seemed like he was living in a different world, always looking over his shoulder. What finally brought Duc to seek help was a moment at the hardware store: he saw a patrol car in the parking lot and felt his throat close up. He stood frozen for almost a minute before walking out without buying anything. That night, he admitted to his wife that he was afraid all the time, and that the fear was making him do things he knew did not make sense. He was terrified that his own mind was becoming his worst enemy, and he no longer knew how to stop the feedback loop between the constant alarm in his body and the desperate, failing ways he tried to quiet it.
